title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban
text:
Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.
Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.
Backed by £9.3m of funding from Wellcome and working with more than 300,000 young people across Britain, researchers hope to provide crucial answers for those working on online safety and digital policy.
“We all know there has been a quite heated debate around the social media ban here in the UK [and] also around the world, but there is very limited scientific evidence about how social media and its restrictions [are] actually affecting the mental health of young people,” said Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome.
Iannone said restrictions will offer a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media affects young people’s mental health.
“We really don’t think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don’t work,” she said. “Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people’s digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing.”
Australia brought in a social media ban for under-16s last year, and other countries are also taking action,including Canada, Greece, and Denmark.
In the UK, a social media ban for under-16s is expected in the spring, barring children from platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X. There will also be restrictions around live-streaming and contact from strangers on gaming platforms.
Opinions have been split, with some raising concerns about the impact on young people who rely on social media for friendships, white others point out children could find ways around bans.
One project in the study is called Smart Schools Plus and is co-led by Prof Victoria Goodyear of the University of Birmingham. The research will span 16 schools and 800 pupils in England, focusing not only on mental health and wellbeing, but also on physical activity, sleep, social networks, disruptive school behaviour, attainment, and attendance. As part of the work, the team will use surveys, apps, interviews, digital diaries and research-grade activity trackers.
“We’re going to look at whether sleep, physical activity, social networks, and these other educational outcomes influence the mental health outcomes,” Goodyear said. “So it’s answering, why are there any changes or why are there not any changes?”
The team will explore whether risky content – such as material relating to self-harm, suicide and eating disorders – has moved from one online platform to another as a result of the ban.
Another project, co-led by Dr Gemma Knowles of King’s College London, will explore whether the ban’s impacts differ for young people of different genders, social class, and sexual orientations.
Meanwhile, Dr Alex Kwong from the University of Edinburgh said his team will work with families across England, Wales and Scotland.
“We’re interested in understanding how these social media restrictions impact children and families together,” he said. “So, understanding if that will then lead to potential conflict and how families then navigate the battle.”
The team will also look at whether young people find workarounds for the restrictions. “If children and adolescents still use social media after the ban, that’s the difference between understanding policy on paper and policy in practice,” Kwong said.
